LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Worried, Relieved, Jealous & Embarrassed — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson names the four feelings children hide: the worry that whispers, the relief that lands, the jealousy that burns and the embarrassment that blushes — all of them normal, all of them nameable.

What is this?

Worried is a what-if that will not stop, relieved is the phew when the worry ends, jealous is the hot wish for what someone else has, and embarrassed is the blush when everyone is looking.

What does it mean?

Jealous and embarrassed are the loneliest feelings of preschool — children carry them secretly, sure they are the only ones. The cure is not a lecture; it is a grown-up saying "I felt that too, last Tuesday."

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: worried is the brain trying to protect you (it just over-protects); jealous means you noticed something you want — and wants can be talked about; and embarrassed shrinks fastest when someone kind stays normal beside you.

Why this matters

This is the class’s bravest card: the feelings children least want to admit are the ones most worth naming together. A child who can say "I am jealous" at four is learning to bring shadows into the light — for life.

What it teaches

Worry literacy (naming the what-ifs), relief recognition (marking safety), envy vocabulary (jealousy as information about wants), and shame prevention — the early inoculation that embarrassment is universal and survivable.

Words to learn

worriedrelievedjealousembarrassedwhat iftricky feelingsnormal

Say this to your child

“"Some feelings play hide-and-seek. Worried is the what-if feeling: what if the dark, what if the first day, what if nobody plays with me — your brain is trying to protect you; it just shouts sometimes. Relieved is what lands after: phew — the worry was bigger than the thing. Jealous is the hot one: my friend has it and I want it TOO — that feeling is just information about a want, and wants can be said out loud. And embarrassed is the blush: everyone looking, wishing they would stop. Here is the secret about all four: every single person feels them — me, you, the neighbours, everyone. Named out loud, they get small. That is the whole trick."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "The four tricky feelings — everyone has them."
  2. Read the panels: the finger-to-mouth boy is WORRIED, the eyes-closed relieved girl just felt the phew, the crossed-arms boy is JEALOUS, the blushing hunched girl is EMBARRASSED.
  3. Tell the grown-up stories below — one real, light story per feeling, told with a smile not a shadow.
  4. Practise the relief sound: "phew" — said out loud with wiped brows; relief deserves its own word.
  5. Close with the takeaway: "tricky feelings are not bad feelings — they are just shy. Named, they behave."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the tricky feelings: Worried, a boy with a finger to his mouth; Relieved, a girl with closed eyes and hands clasped in relief; Jealous, a sulking boy with crossed arms; and Embarrassed, a blushing girl hunched with clasped hands — every one drawn kindly, none of them caricatured.

Ask your child

"What does worried whisper?" "What sound does relieved make?" "What is jealous telling you?" "What helps embarrassed most?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Worried is a what-if!" "Phew!" (marking their own relief) or the confession: "I felt jealous when she had the bigger cake."

Out in the real world

Tricky feelings visit weekly: the stormy night (worried), the found toy (relieved), the sibling’s bigger slice (jealous), the potty accident at a friend’s house (embarrassed). Meet each one at its address — name it lightly, tell yours, move on. The lightness is the lesson.

Try it together

Grown-Up Story Swap: one feeling a night, four nights. The grown-up tells one true, small story — a worry that turned out fine, a jealous moment, an embarrassing tumble — told lightly, laughed WITH not at. Then the child may swap one of their own or just listen. No lessons attached; the stories do the teaching, and the safety does the rest.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which feeling says what-if? Which one says phew? Are the tricky feelings normal?" Worried, relieved, yes — three answers and the shyest feelings are out of hiding.

Parent tips

Never say "you have nothing to be embarrassed about" — to a blushing child that is one more person looking. Instead, stay normal: sit beside, carry on gently, let the moment pass in good company. And treat jealousy as a wants-report, not a character flaw: "you noticed you wanted that. Wants can be spoken. Want to tell me about it?"

This lesson pairs with the Worried, Relieved, Jealous & Embarrassed flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
